Q: What is more 'Pythonic' for 'not'? A:

Although 4 not in a is to be preferred when the choice is made in isolation, there can be cases when the other choice not 4 in a is to be preferred.

For example, if the specification for the software is written to match not 4 in a, then it might be best to leave it matching the specification to aid when checking the software against the specification.

A further example is that one way allows this expression of deteriorating health:

( 4 in well,
  well,
  not well,
  not 4 in well) #!

Q: polars.read_csv vs polars.read_csv_batched vs polars.scan_csv? A:

polars.scan_csv produces a query plan (called a LazyFrame). You can then build you query and on the end call collect to materialize a DataFrame.

This is the case for all scan_ methods. The benefit of this is that the Polars optimizer then can push down optimizations into the readers. It can apply filters in the readers and only selects columns it needs. This can save a lot of work.

polars.read_csv can be seen as polars.scan_csv().collect(). E.g. you simply read all the data and immediately produce a DataFrame. This means that you might do work that was not needed. The Polars optimizer is not able to do anything if you want a result immediately.

I don't agree with the other answer that polars.read_csv only should be used when data is large. It is just as well suitable for smaller data.

Q: Filling multiple columns at once with polars' map_elements A:

Your function returns list of values, so you have to call it accordingly:

df.with_columns(
    pl.struct(pl.all())
      .map_elements(my_complicated_function, pl.List(pl.Int64))
      .list.to_struct(fields=["column1","column2","column3"])
      .alias("result")
).unnest("result")

Or, if you can change your function so it returns dictionary:

def my_complicated_function(row):

     # ...

     return {"column1": value1, "column2": value2, "column3": value3}

You can get return value into struct directly, so you have names of the columns defined inside of your function and then pl.DataFrame.unnest()

df.with_columns(
    pl.struct(pl.all())
      .map_elements(my_complicated_function, return_dtype=pl.Struct)
      .alias("result")
).unnest("result")

Q: High SQL Server parse and compile time with UDF A:

This issue is due to the SQL Server inline UDF feature.

There are multiple reasons why this function is not considered inlinable in my version of SQL Server 2022 but it looks like these are not included in the fixes in your 2019 version.

(In the tsql_scalar_udf_not_inlineable extended event I see blocked reason of MultipleReturns initially and then blocked reason of ExprReEval if I comment out the first return)

When it inlines it you end up with something like this (indicative code only)

SELECT REPLACE(V9.sName, 'WR','R')
FROM (VALUES('s8da40f')) V0(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN right(V0.sName, 3) IN(' JR',' SR') THEN  SUBSTRING(V0.sName , 1, len(V0.sName )-3) ELSE V0.sName END)) v1(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN right(V1.sName, 1) IN('S','Z')  AND PATINDEX('%[^SZ]%', V1.sName) > 0 THEN  SUBSTRING(V1.sName, 1, LEN(V1.sName) - (PATINDEX('%[^SZ]%', REVERSE(V1.sName)) -1)) ELSE V1.sName END)) v2(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN LEFT(V2.sName, 3) = 'MAC' THEN  'MC' + SUBSTRING(V2.sName, 4, LEN(V2.sName)) ELSE V2.sName END)) V3(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN LEFT(V3.sName, 2) = 'PF' THEN 'F' + SUBSTRING(V3.sName, 3, LEN(V3.sName))  ELSE V3.sName END)) V4(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN RIGHT(V4.sName, 2) = 'IX' THEN SUBSTRING(V4.sName, 1, LEN(V4.sName) - 2) + 'IC'  ELSE V4.sName END)) V5(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN RIGHT(V5.sName, 2) = 'EX' THEN SUBSTRING(V5.sName, 1, LEN(V5.sName) - 2) + 'EC'  ELSE V5.sName END)) V6(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN RIGHT(V6.sName, 2) IN('YE','EE','IE')  THEN SUBSTRING(V6.sName, 1, LEN(V6.sName) - 2) + 'Y'  ELSE V6.sName END)) V7(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN RIGHT(V7.sName, 2) IN('NT','ND') THEN  SUBSTRING(V7.sName, 1, LEN(V7.sName) - 2) + 'N' ELSE V7.sName END)) V8(sName)
CROSS APPLY (VALUES(CASE WHEN RIGHT(V8.sName, 2) IN('DT','RT', 'RD') THEN  SUBSTRING(V8.sName, 1, LEN(V8.sName) - 2) + 'D' ELSE V8.sName END)) V9(sName)

which it then struggles to optimize. (If I try and run the query above I see "Internal error: An expression services limit has been reached. Please look for potentially complex expressions in your query, and try to simplify them.")

The call stack when this error is hit is

On SQL Server 2019 (RTM) - 15.0.2000.5 localdb if I try and run your original function query I see the huge compilation time but then the actual execution plan generated shows that the CompileTime was tiny and the actual execution plan does not have the function inlined.

During the attempt to compile the function it ends up raising an error with this call stack. This is not returned to the user but is when it gives up and just creates a plan with the non inlined function call.

You can disable inlining for that function or consider rewriting it to make it less complex if it is inlined.

Q: How to use a function returning a tuple to add multiple columns to data frame in Polars A:

To answer the question as asked you can do this:

(
    df
    .with_columns(pl.col('a').map_elements(f).alias('temp'))
    .with_columns(pl.col('temp').list.to_struct(fields=['b','c']))
    .unnest('temp')
    .with_columns(pl.col('b','c').cast(pl.Int32))
)

You can't chain the list.to_struct in the same with_columns as the map_elements. I think it has to do with map_elements looping on each element so it isn't, for lack of a better term, a fully formed column yet. If you want the output to be a specific dtype, you have to cast it after you unnest.

That being said, using map_elements is an anti-pattern and should be avoided wherever possible as it undoes all of the optimizations that make polars fast. Ideally you'd convert your f into polars expressions. If there's no way to make f into polars expressions but it can be vectorized then use map_batches instead of map_elements.
